analysis.one_liner: Caps medical malpractice awards while adding tax credits for health insurance and safety-net funding.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate Majority Leader on July 27, 2005, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have done two big things at once. It would have rewritten medical malpractice lawsuits nationwide: capping compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000, limiting lawyers' fees, making it harder to win punitive damages, and reducing payouts by any insurance the victim already receives. At the same time, it would have created a refundable tax credit to help people buy health insurance, offered tax breaks for high-deductible plans and health savings accounts, funded outreach to sign children up for public coverage, and expanded grants for community health centers and high-risk insurance pools.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers and medical providers would gain the most from the malpractice limits, since caps on pain-and-suffering awards and lawyers' fees shrink payouts. Uninsured people would gain a refundable, advanceable tax credit toward premiums, small-business employees would get a credit toward health savings accounts, children eligible for public coverage would benefit from enrollment grants, and residents of underserved areas would gain from new health center funding. People with medical conditions that make private insurance unaffordable would benefit from continued high-risk pool funding.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable, advanceable tax credit for health insurance premiums, paid directly to insurers so people could use it at purchase time [S2][S3].
Allows a tax deduction for premiums under high-deductible health plans and a refundable credit for small employers' contributions to employees' health savings accounts [S2].
Funds innovative outreach and enrollment efforts to sign children up for Medicaid and SCHIP, and lets states use simplified income determinations for kids' coverage [S2].
Grants for community health centers in high-need areas, coverage of integrated health center services under Medicare and Medicaid, and reauthorization of state high-risk insurance pools [S2].
Supporters argued malpractice caps would lower malpractice insurance premiums and reduce 'defensive medicine,' lowering overall health costs [S3].

Creates an Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology and authorizes $125 million in startup funding to build a nationwide system for exchanging medical records electronically [S3].
Lets medical students get forbearance on loans for volunteering at free clinics, and raises the prospect of student-loan forbearance for physicians serving free clinics [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical negligence would bear the largest cost: compensation for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and loss of enjoyment of life would be capped at $250,000 no matter how severe the injury, and awards would be reduced by any insurance or benefits the victim already receives. Federal taxpayers would fund the new tax credits and grants. State trial courts and the plaintiffs' bar would lose fee income and punitive-damage leverage, and states would lose control over their own malpractice rules where federal law preempts them.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages applies to every patient regardless of injury severity; children, retirees, and people not earning wages — who have small economic losses but severe suffering — would see the deepest cuts in compensation, and the jury would not even be told a cap exists [S3].

Damages would be reduced dollar-for-dollar by any health insurance, disability, or workers' compensation benefits the injured patient was entitled to, meaning patients who were already insured would recover less than uninsured ones for the same injury [S3].

The subtitle would preempt state laws that allow larger damages or longer filing periods, overriding state choices about their own courts, while simultaneously allowing state laws that give providers greater protections to stand — the asymmetry runs one way [S3].

Punitive damages would require 'clear and convincing' proof of malicious intent or deliberate disregard, be capped at $250,000 or twice economic damages, and could not even be pleaded in the initial filing — making the rare worst cases nearly impossible to punish [S3].

The tax credits for high-deductible plans and health savings accounts deliver the largest benefits to people with enough income to owe taxes or fund accounts, and the bill includes no cost controls on premiums themselves [S3].
Punitive damages would require clear and convincing proof of malicious intent, capped at $250,000 or twice economic damages, and could not be raised in the initial lawsuit filing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage and safety-net pieces were real but modest, and the tax credits leaned toward people who could already afford high-deductible plans. The centerpiece, by size and ambition, was the malpractice rewrite, and its costs fell on exactly the people the bill's coverage provisions were meant to help: a patient harmed by malpractice who had health insurance would see damages cut twice over, once by the cap and once by the collateral-source offset. A fair reading is a bill that traded the legal rights of injured patients for premium subsidies and industry liability relief, with genuine but secondary gains for children's enrollment and community clinics.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so the bill died quietly when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Frist, then Senate Majority Leader, introduced the bill on July 27, 2005 with nine Republican cosponsors including Mitch McConnell, Judd Gregg, and Michael Enzi [S1][S4][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].
The bill's tax, Medicare, and Medicaid provisions fell squarely within the Finance Committee's jurisdiction, giving that committee control over its fate [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held. Injured patients kept the existing malpractice rules in their states, and malpractice insurers and provider groups did not get the caps they sought. On the other side, the uninsured got no tax credits, children got no new enrollment funding, and community health centers got no expansion — the bill's friendly provisions died with its unfriendly ones.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients; the uninsured got nothing

sides.party_line_note: All ten Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat is recorded as supporting or acting on the bill; with Republicans holding 55 Senate seats, the bill never came to a vote.

industries.note: Caps on noneconomic damages, punitive damages, and lawyer fees would directly reduce what insurers pay out on claims. The cost of that savings falls on patients with severe injuries, whose compensation would be capped at $250,000 for pain and suffering.

Providers would gain liability caps and a five-year exemption from federal anti-kickback and self-referral rules so hospitals and vendors could give them health IT equipment and software. They would also face new Medicare value-based payment measurement.

The refundable, advanceable premium tax credit would route public subsidy dollars through private insurers, making them the channel for federally supported coverage. High-deductible plans and HSAs would steer more customers into insurer-administered products.

The bill authorizes $125 million for a nationwide interoperable health records system and creates a five-year safe harbor from anti-kickback rules for vendors providing systems to providers, opening a federally supported market for EHR software.

Sliding-scale caps on contingency fees and new limits on expert testimony and punitive claims would cut the fees and win rates of lawyers who represent malpractice victims. Their interest here runs with injured patients' recovery.
